q: Tell me about a time you were criticised in front of other people. How did you respond?
ans: Interviewer is assessing: composure, maturity, and whether you protect relationships under social pressure. In STAR, describe the setting, your immediate reaction (staying calm), what you did afterwards, such as asking for a private follow-up, and the result. Illustrative example (replace with your own facts): 'During [review or presentation] I was told [criticism]. I stayed calm, acknowledged the point, and later asked [person] for specifics. I applied the feedback and [outcome].'
fu: What would you say to someone who criticises in public?
How did you feel, honestly?

q: Tell me about a time a junior or peer you considered less experienced pointed out a flaw in your work.
ans: Interviewer is assessing: humility and willingness to learn from anyone. In STAR, describe the flaw, how you reacted internally, how you verified the claim, and what you did. Show you value correctness over status. Illustrative example (replace with your facts): 'A junior teammate noticed [issue] in [work]. I checked it, found they were right, thanked them, fixed it, and added [check] to avoid repeats.'
fu: How do you encourage others to speak up?
What if they had been wrong?

q: Tell me about an ethical dilemma you faced in college or on a project and how you handled it.
ans: Interviewer is assessing: integrity, judgment, and the courage to act. In STAR, describe the dilemma, the options and their consequences, the principle that guided you, what you did, and the outcome. Pick a real situation such as academic honesty or data use. Illustrative example (replace with your own): 'In [situation] I could have [shortcut], but that would have [harm]. I chose [action], explained my reasons, and [outcome].'
cm: Hiding the cost of doing the right thing
fu: What would you do if the same situation repeated?
Did it cost you anything?

q: Describe a time someone asked you to share your work or answers in a way you were uncomfortable with. What did you do?
ans: Interviewer is assessing: boundaries, honesty, and tact. In STAR, describe the request, why it was a problem, how you declined or offered an appropriate alternative such as explaining concepts, and the outcome for the relationship. Illustrative example (replace with your own): 'A friend asked for my [assignment] to copy. I declined, offered to explain the concept instead, and they [outcome]. It taught me to hold a boundary kindly.'
fu: What if it was your close friend?
How would you handle a manager asking?

q: Tell me about a time you saw someone behaving unethically. What did you do?
ans: Interviewer is assessing: moral courage and sensible escalation. In STAR, describe what you observed, how you confirmed the facts, who you approached (the person directly or an appropriate authority), and the result. Avoid dramatic or unverifiable stories. Illustrative example (replace with your facts): 'I noticed [behaviour]. I first verified [fact], spoke with [person or authority], and the issue was [outcome]. I learned the value of checking facts before escalating.'
fu: What if your manager was the one involved?
How do you protect yourself when reporting?

q: Tell me about a time you had to learn an unfamiliar technology quickly for a project.
ans: Interviewer is assessing: learning agility and method. In STAR, describe the project need, your learning plan (documentation, small prototype, asking for help), how you applied it, and the result. Mention how you verified understanding. Illustrative example (replace with your own): 'We needed [technology] for [project] within [time]. I read the docs, built a small prototype, asked [person] to review, and we delivered [outcome].'
cm: Not mentioning how you checked understanding
fu: How do you decide when you know enough to start?
What went wrong while learning?

q: Describe a time you taught yourself something difficult without a teacher or structured course.
ans: Interviewer is assessing: self-direction, persistence, and metacognition. In STAR, explain why you needed the skill, how you structured your own learning (resources, practice, feedback), obstacles, and the demonstrable result. Illustrative example (replace with your facts): 'I wanted to learn [skill]. I set weekly goals, built [project], tested myself by [method], and now I can [outcome].'
fu: How do you stay consistent?
How would you teach it to someone else?

q: Tell me about a time you had to understand an unfamiliar codebase or system using only documentation and exploration.
ans: Interviewer is assessing: investigative skills and independence. In STAR, describe the task, how you explored (reading structure, running it, tracing a request, writing notes), when you asked for help, and the result. Illustrative example (replace with your own): 'I needed to modify [system]. I traced [flow], documented [findings], asked [person] one precise question, and shipped [change].'
cm: Waiting for someone to explain everything
Not asking for help at all
fu: What would you document for the next person?
How do you avoid breaking things?

q: Describe a time you delivered something important under intense time pressure.
ans: Interviewer is assessing: prioritisation, composure, and quality under stress. In STAR, set the stakes and time limit, explain how you prioritised and simplified, what you did to maintain quality, and the result. Illustrative example (replace with your own facts): 'With [hours or days] left for [deliverable], I focused on [core features], dropped [nice-to-have], tested [critical path], and we submitted [outcome].'
fu: What did you cut and why?
What would you do to avoid the crunch next time?

q: Tell me about a high-stakes moment, such as a demo, viva, or presentation, and how you prepared and performed.
ans: Interviewer is assessing: preparation habits and composure. In STAR, describe the event and its importance, how you prepared (rehearsals, contingency plans), what happened on the day, and the outcome plus lesson. Illustrative example (replace with your facts): 'For [event] I rehearsed [times], prepared for [likely questions], and when [problem] happened I [response]. The result was [outcome].'
fu: What would you do differently?
How do you manage nerves?

q: Tell me about a time something went wrong at the last minute and how you stayed calm.
ans: Interviewer is assessing: crisis response and communication. In STAR, describe the failure, how you assessed what mattered, the immediate actions, how you communicated with others, and the outcome. Illustrative example (replace with your own): 'Just before [deadline] [problem] occurred. I assessed [impact], fixed [critical part] first, informed [person], and we recovered by [result].'
fu: What did you learn about prevention?
What would you tell your team in that moment?

q: Tell me about a time your estimate of the work turned out to be wrong, and how you still managed to deliver.
ans: Interviewer is assessing: planning realism, adaptability, and honest communication. In STAR, explain the original estimate, when and how you discovered the gap, what you did (re-scope, ask for help, communicate), and what you changed in future estimates. Illustrative example (replace with your facts): 'I estimated [time] for [task] but [cause] added [work]. I told [person], re-scoped to [core], and delivered [outcome]. I now add buffers.'
fu: How do you estimate now?
What signals told you the estimate was off?

q: Describe a time you had to negotiate or change a deadline. How did you approach it?
ans: Interviewer is assessing: negotiation, professionalism, and trade-off thinking. In STAR, describe why the deadline was unrealistic, how you gathered facts, what options you offered (reduced scope, phased delivery), and the agreed outcome. Illustrative example (replace with your own facts): 'The deadline for [task] was not feasible because [reason]. I proposed [options] with timelines and [person] agreed to [outcome].'
fu: What if they had refused?
How early did you raise it?

q: Tell me about a time a teammate's delay put your deadline at risk. What did you do?
ans: Interviewer is assessing: dependency management and constructive communication. In STAR, describe the dependency, how you checked in with the teammate to understand the cause, how you offered help or adjusted the plan, and the result. Illustrative example (replace with your facts): 'My part depended on [teammate's task]. I asked what was blocking it, offered [help], adjusted my plan, and we delivered [outcome].'
fu: When would you involve the manager?
How do you track dependencies?

q: Tell me about a time a code review or evaluation pointed out serious flaws in your work.
ans: Interviewer is assessing: coachability and quality mindset. In STAR, describe the work and the feedback, your reaction, how you addressed each point, and how your later work changed. Illustrative example (replace with your own): 'A review of [work] found [flaws]. I listed every point, fixed them, asked about [standard], and in later work I [improvement]. The reviewer noted [result].'
fu: What was the hardest point to accept?
How do you review your own work now?

q: Describe feedback you initially disagreed with but later realised was right.
ans: Interviewer is assessing: self-awareness and openness. In STAR, describe the feedback, why you disagreed, what changed your mind (evidence or experience), and how you acted. Show you can revise your view. Illustrative example (replace with your facts): 'I was told [feedback] and thought [disagreement]. After [event] I saw they were right. I changed [behaviour] and thanked them.'
cm: Choosing feedback that was obviously right
fu: How do you decide whether feedback is valid?
What if you still disagree?

q: Tell me about a time you asked for feedback and it was tougher than you expected.
ans: Interviewer is assessing: growth mindset and resilience. In STAR, explain why you asked, what you heard, how you processed the emotional reaction, what actions you took, and the result. Illustrative example (replace with your own): 'I asked [person] about my [work]. They said [tough point]. I took time to reflect, made a plan to [action], and later [outcome].'
fu: How do you ask for feedback?
What was the most useful sentence you heard?

q: Tell me about a mistake you made that affected other people. How did you handle it?
ans: Interviewer is assessing: accountability, honesty, and recovery. In STAR, describe the mistake, how you realised it, how you informed those affected, what you did to fix it, and what you changed. Do not minimise or blame. Illustrative example (replace with your facts): 'I made [mistake] in [work], which affected [people]. I told them immediately, helped fix [part], and now I [new check].'
fu: How did the team react?
What system would have caught it?

q: Describe a time you noticed a mistake in your work after you had already submitted it.
ans: Interviewer is assessing: integrity and proactive correction. In STAR, describe what you found, whether you reported it, how you corrected it, and how you prevented it in future. Show you prefer disclosing early to hoping nobody notices. Illustrative example (replace with your own): 'After submitting [work] I found [error]. I informed [person], submitted a correction, and now I run [check] before submitting.'
fu: What if disclosing had cost you marks or credit?
What check would you add?

q: Tell me about a time a team effort failed and you had to take responsibility for your part.
ans: Interviewer is assessing: balanced accountability, not self-blame or scapegoating. In STAR, describe the failure, your specific contribution to it, how you acknowledged it to the team, and what you did to repair and improve. Illustrative example (replace with your facts): 'Our [project] failed partly because I [your part]. I acknowledged it in [setting], proposed [fix], and in the next project we [improvement].'
fu: How did the team respond?
What would you do differently on day one?
